data.title: CJI Surya Kant calls for guidelines on AI use, disclosure in legal research
data.description:
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Saturday urged the Commonwealth Legal Education Association (CLEA) to develop model guidelines on the disclosure of AI assistance in legal research.

Delivering the inaugural address at CLEA 1st Annual International Conference on Legal Education 2026 here, he also suggested that a minimum period of legal aid work be made compulsory for every student to graduate, with additional credits for those who go beyond it.

"I would urge CLEA to take the lead by developing model guidelines on the disclosure of AI assistance in legal research, which law schools and journals across the Commonwealth could adapt to their own needs," he said.

 

Talking about research in the age of AI, he cautioned that no student should be held guilty of misconduct on the word of a machine alone as software that claims to tell whether a given essay was written by a student or by a machine can go wrong for different reasons.

Students must know which uses are permitted and which must be disclosed, among others.

He said tools like AI can help researchers find and organise material, but the answer is not necessarily an accurate one.

However, he said that shortcomings like a fabricated authority looking entirely plausible may occur when using these technological tools.

The answer lies in responsible use, and not in uncritical adoption or blanket prohibition.

The researchers must check every authority against its primary source, disclose any material assistance, and remain answerable for what they publish, he said.

An AI system cannot be credited as an author, precisely because it cannot be held responsible for the work.

He said generative artificial intelligence has unsettled the long-held assumption that an examination sheet or a research paper is evidence of what a student knows.

A tool can now summarise a judgment, suggest arguments, and produce a polished answer within minutes.

"The question, therefore, is no longer whether students will use these tools, but whether the work they submit still reflects their own reasoning, understanding, and appreciation for the law," Justice Surya Kant said.

The simplest response would be to ban such tools altogether, but he is convinced that this would be neither practicable nor wise, he said.

Courts across the Commonwealth have largely chosen to regulate the use of such tools rather than forbid them.

The Supreme Court of Singapore, for instance, permits court users to employ such tools, but holds them fully responsible for everything they file, he said.

He said a ban would only drive this use out of sight, where it can be neither guided nor examined.

"The wiser course is to set clear rules and to teach responsible use, so that technology assists the student's search," he said.

He said many institutions now rely on software that claims to tell whether a given essay was written by a student or by a machine, and it is tempting to treat its verdict as proof of misconduct.

The software used to determine whether an essay was written by the student or not is far from reliable.

He cited a 2023 study which found that seven widely used detectors, though almost flawless with essays written by schoolchildren in the US, wrongly flagged more than three in every five essays by non-native speakers of English as machine generated.

In a Commonwealth where so many students write in English as a second or third language, an honest student could thus be branded a cheat on the strength of a number that no one can explain, and that student cannot meaningfully challenge, he said.

Justice Surya Kant said assessment, too, must evolve, so that written work is supported by an oral explanation, a defence of the authorities relied upon, or an exercise in spotting the errors in a machine-generated answer.

Talking about the importance of legal aid clinics, he said the legal services authority's own scheme points the way, envisaging panel lawyers and para-legal volunteers working alongside students, and clinics that reach out to villages and settlements.

However, he believes that a clinic's work should also not pause with the semester, and students who serve in it during their breaks should receive certificates for the work they actually do, he said.

Legal aid clinics can themselves become centres of continuing learning, where panel advocates, legal services officers and students meet in regular case discussions, he said.

On the question of whether practical learning should remain confined to a separate corner of the curriculum, or whether it should also shape the teaching of core subjects such as Evidence, Criminal Procedure, Family Law and Constitutional Law, he said the latter deserves serious consideration.

With 'uniform citation for the commonwealth' being the topic for a technical session of the conference, he said where a Court has assigned a neutral citation, as the Supreme Court has done since 2023, that citation should serve as its principal identifier.

A shared minimum format, giving the year, the Court, the decision number and the paragraph, would then allow any judgment to be traced and verified across borders, he added.

data.title: Bihar now known for development, not scams and crimes: PM targets Cong-RJD
data.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday made a stinging attack on the opposition RJD-Congress alliance in Bihar, asserting that the state, under the NDA's rule, was making news for development and investments "in place of scams and crimes".

Modi addressed a rally in Jafarpatti of Vaishali district, about 50 km from the state capital, where he dedicated to the nation projects worth more than ₹34,000 crore, including a bridge over the Ganga. The bridge has been named 'Nitish Setu'.

The PM, who delivered a relatively short speech, said that he was short on time and had to visit the adjoining Uttar Pradesh.

 

He said the bridge was named after the JD(U) president, who gave up the post of chief minister in April to make way for a BJP-helmed government, "as a mark of respect for his contributions to the state".

"The state has come a long way since the NDA took over. Earlier, only scams and crimes were talked about. Now Bihar makes news for investment proposals and action taken against those who indulge in any type of wrongdoing," he said.

Modi, who was speaking in an area falling under the Hajipur Lok Sabha constituency, represented by Union minister Chirag Paswan, also recalled the contributions of the latter's late father Ram Vilas Paswan, who had represented the parliamentary seat several times.

The PM also trained his guns at the Congress, accusing it of having "misled people with slogans of garibi hatao", drawing a contrast with the NDA government at the Centre over the last 12 years during which "50 crore people have moved out of the clutches of poverty".

data.title: Noel Tata's salvo sets stage for stormy Tata Sons board meet next week
data.description:
Tata Trusts Chairman and Tata Sons nominee director Noel Tata has renewed his demand for the audio and video recordings of a contentious board meeting of the group holding company held on September 17, 2026, while questioning the validity of N Chandrasekaran's reappointment and flagging alleged conflict-of-interest concerns involving nominee director Venu Srinivasan.
 
In a fresh letter dated November 20, addressed to Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, company secretary and group corporate secretary at Tata Sons, and copied to all directors, including chairman Chandrasekaran, Noel expressed disappointment with the company's response to his earlier requests for the recordings and other documents.
 
The latest communication comes days before the next Tata Sons board meeting, scheduled for November 26, at which the minutes of the September 17 meeting are expected to come up for confirmation.
 
 
"Of the requests made in my letter of 26 October 2026, you have furnished two documents: a notice of interest dated 10 April 2025 and the agenda and unsigned minutes of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee. The remaining requests are either refused or passed over," Noel wrote.
 
Noel pointed out that Mukhopadhyay's earlier response had confirmed that an audio and video recording of the September 17 board meeting had been made.
 
The company secretary had said the recording was intended to assist in preparing the draft minutes, that sharing such recordings was not company practice and that they were not required to be retained or shared with anyone, including directors.
 
Noel said this position was unacceptable.
 
"My request is not founded on practice. It is made because the draft minutes are disputed on the most important matter that came before the board that day, and because the recording is the only record of what was said that was not written by anyone," he wrote.
 
He argued that a director was entitled to inspect the company's books and records, whether maintained in physical or electronic form, and that neither the law nor the Articles of Association entitled Tata Sons to withhold the recording of a board meeting attended by the director.
 
"Your statement that the recording is not required to be retained is of serious concern," he wrote.
 
Noel has asked the company to confirm that the complete audio and video recording of the September 17 meeting exists in its original and unedited form, along with its metadata.
 
He has also sought details of where the recording is held, who is responsible for its custody and who has accessed it since September 17. He wants the company to confirm that the recording will be preserved until all questions concerning the meeting have been resolved.
 
If any part of the recording has been deleted, edited or overwritten, Noel has sought details of when the action was taken, by whom and on whose instructions.
 
The letter warned that Tata Sons had been aware since September 18 that the record of the meeting was disputed and that the recording was required.
 
"Any deletion or alteration of it after that date would be the deliberate destruction of evidence, and every person responsible for it would be personally answerable," Noel wrote.
 
He offered to inspect the recording at Bombay House, accompanied by an adviser and in the presence of Mukhopadhyay. He also sought a transcript prepared by an independent stenographer at his expense before November 25.
 
Noel has also questioned whether his dissent at the September 17 meeting was properly recorded. He sought details of when the minutes were entered in the minutes book and who had signed them.
 
He pointed out that the minutes were required to be entered within 30 days of the meeting and said he had still not received the final signed record.
 
Referring to item 9 of the board meeting agenda concerning the proposed reappointment of Chandrasekaran as executive chairman, Noel argued that Chandrasekaran had an interest in the matter and should not participate in settling or signing the minutes relating to it.
 
"Chandrasekaran is interested in that item" and therefore "he cannot properly decide what the minutes of that item should say, or sign them as a true record over my objection," Noel wrote.
 
"Needless to add that Mr. N. Chandrasekaran should take no part in settling or signing the record of item 9," he added.
 
Noel also questioned the process through which the resolution to appoint Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for another five-year term was moved.
 
He alleged that the resolution was introduced without prior notice and on the basis of a recommendation that had not yet been made by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC).
 
"The obligation under Section 117 is to file a resolution that has been passed. It does not make valid a resolution that was not," Noel wrote.
 
He also challenged the interpretation of Articles 118 and 121 of the company's Articles of Association.
 
According to Noel, Article 121 requires the affirmative vote of a majority of directors appointed under Article 104B who are present at the meeting.
 
He said there were two such directors and one had voted against the resolution. He disputed the company's reliance on the chairman's casting vote, arguing that Article 121 provides for a casting vote in the event of an equality of votes across the board and does not permit it to override the voting requirement applicable to the two directors appointed under Article 104B.
 
The letter also raised questions over an alleged conflict of interest involving Chandrasekaran's family and Venu Srinivasan, a Tata Sons nominee director and chairman of the TVS Group.
 
Noel said the disclosure available to the Tata Sons board recorded that Chandrasekaran's wife and son were partners in Hanno Infra LLP and directors and members of Hanno One Warehousing Private Limited.
 
However, he alleged that the disclosure did not mention any business dealings with TVS Motor Company.
 
The issue assumes significance amid reported commercial dealings between TVS Motor and Hanno One, an entity linked to Chandrasekaran's family.
 
Noel questioned whether Srinivasan could independently assess Chandrasekaran's performance, recommend his remuneration and vote on his reappointment while a company associated with Srinivasan and his family had a continuing commercial relationship with an entity linked to Chandrasekaran's family.
 
"The question is whether a director who was called upon to assess the performance of the executive chairman, to recommend his remuneration and to vote on his reappointment could do so with independent judgment while the company which he and his family lead was in a continuing commercial relationship with a company owned by the executive chairman's wife and son," Noel wrote.
 
He pointed out that the minutes provided to him showed that Srinivasan had participated in the committee that reviewed Chandrasekaran's performance and recommended his remuneration on June 12, 2026, and subsequently decided on September 3 to ask him to continue as chairman.
 
Noel also cited the Tata Code of Conduct, arguing that it required disclosure where a relationship could, on an objective assessment, raise concerns over a potential conflict of interest.
 
Tata Sons has previously rejected allegations of a conflict of interest involving the two families and maintained that the relevant disclosures had been made. The latest letter seeks further clarity on the matter.
 
The proposed listing of Tata Sons remains another major point of disagreement between Noel and the company's management.
 
In his latest communication, Noel referred to the Reserve Bank of India's November 16 letter asking Tata Sons to comply with the applicable regulatory requirements, including listing.
 
He said the RBI's response followed a letter sent by Tata Sons on October 6, which had not been placed before the board or shown to him before being dispatched.
 
"That letter was not placed before the board or shown to me before it was sent, and I have not seen it," Noel wrote.
 
He has sought a copy of the October 6 communication, details of who approved it and whether it was shown to any director before being sent.
 
Noel also wants to know what Tata Sons communicated to the RBI about the board's September 17 discussions on the listing issue.
 
He said the company was supposed to seek the RBI's guidance on his alternative restructuring proposal, which was aimed at allowing Tata Sons to remain privately held.
 
"Please tell me whether the company placed that proposal before the Reserve Bank and, if it did not, why not," he wrote.
 
In conclusion, Noel has asked Tata Sons not to take any steps towards listing, including appointing advisers or intermediaries, until the board has considered the alternative proposal to retain the company's privately held status.
 
He has sought the circulation of this proposal, along with the agenda for the November 26 board meeting, and wants the company to seek clarification from the RBI on the specific restructuring proposal.
 
The latest letter adds to the differences between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons over the holding company's ownership structure, regulatory obligations and leadership succession.
 
The November 26 board meeting is expected to be an important forum for addressing the disputed minutes and the questions surrounding Chandrasekaran's reappointment and the proposed listing.

data.title: MCD tightens guest house safety rules, makes fire certificate compulsory
data.description:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has barred guest houses from operating on the fourth floor or above in buildings and tightened fire safety requirements for such establishments as part of a drive to ensure compliance with building norms and safety regulations, officials said on Saturday.

Under the revised directions, guest houses operating in buildings with a height of 12 metres or more must have a valid Fire Safety Certificate (FSC) issued by the Delhi Fire Service.

Senior MCD officials confirmed that the civic body's public health department has directed operators of guest houses and lodging and boarding establishments to comply with the applicable building bye-laws and fire safety requirements.

 

"Operating a guest house without a valid fire safety certificate, or failing to renew it after its expiry, will be treated as a serious safety violation," a senior official said.

Another senior civic official said that all guest houses in the city, regardless of their building height, should come under the fire safety certificate.

Guest houses functioning in buildings below 12 metres in height have been exempted from obtaining an FSC. However, the exemption does not absolve them of their responsibility to follow basic fire safety precautions.

Such establishments must have adequate fire prevention arrangements, unobstructed exit routes and functional fire extinguishers to deal with emergencies, the directions said.

The measures are aimed at ensuring that guest houses maintain basic safety standards and that occupants have adequate protection in case of a fire.

In one of the deadliest incidents this year, a fire broke out in the ground-floor kitchen (originating from an air fryer) of the Flourish Stay Bed and Breakfast hotel in Hauz Rani, killing 22 people, including 13 foreign nationals visiting for medical treatment and 8 members of a single Indian family, and injuring over 40 people.

The establishment was found operating without valid safety licenses.

data.title: India not rogue state: Wangchuk says police lifted curbs after court order
data.description:
Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk on Saturday joined the Leh Apex Body (LAB)-led protest in Leh, alleging that he had been kept under effective house arrest since November 11 and that police withdrew the security deployment outside his residence only after the matter came up before the court.

Addressing a press conference with LAB chairman Chering Dorje Lakruk at the protest site, Wangchuk questioned the legality of the restrictions imposed on his movement and accused the administration of using police personnel to carry out unjustified actions.

He also appealed to President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi to intervene, asserting that constitutional values and democratic freedoms must be upheld.

 

"India is not a rogue state. It is the world's largest democracy, and it has certain constitutional values and standards that must be upheld," he said.

Police on Friday night withdrew arrangements made to ensure compliance with a prohibitory order imposed against Wangchuk in Leh and said Wangchuk had not been placed under house arrest.

Recounting the events of November 11, Wangchuk said he was forcibly picked up while preparations were underway for the indefinite protest to press for resumption of dialogue with the centre and seek deferment of Hill Council polls scheduled for December 4.

"Those who came were wearing masks and hoodies, with their faces concealed. I would hesitate to even call them policemen because they looked more like goons," he said, alleging that although he had agreed to go to jail, he was instead taken to his residence in HIAL, where nearly two dozen local police and CRPF personnel, dressed in commando fatigues and carrying firearms, were deployed.

Wangchuk said he subsequently decided to challenge the restrictions through legal channels with the assistance of lawyers in Delhi and Ladakh.

He said an appeal was filed before the High Court bench in Leh on November 17 and listed for hearing the following day. He claimed that no government representative appeared during the November 18 hearing, following which the court gave the government time until November 19 to submit its response.

The activist stated that Solicitor General of India Tushar Mehta appeared before the court on November 19 and sought time until November 23, which was granted.

"Taking advantage of this time, the authorities withdrew all the personnel deployed outside my residence Friday night," Wangchuk said.

In a post on X, Leh district police said, "Police arrangements which (were) placed to ensure compliance with prohibitory order have been withdrawn. ADM (Additional District magistrate), Leh has passed a prohibitory order against Wangchuk. It is clarified that he was not put under any house arrest as has been claimed." Wangchuk described the police statement as bizarre and questioned how the administration could deny restricting his movement when he had allegedly been prevented from stepping outside his residence.

Wangchuk alleged that the administration was effectively denying restrictions when faced with judicial scrutiny.

"This is an extremely strange way for a government to function. The State is behaving like a rogue state, where anyone can simply be picked up and detained. But when it is required to face the truth in a court of law, it suddenly claims that nothing happened and that there was no such detention," he said, referring to his earlier arrest under NSA.

Wangchuk, however, expressed sympathy for the police personnel and officers deployed outside his residence, alleging that they were being made to carry out actions that could compromise their professional responsibilities.

"I hope that when they joined the civil services, whether the IPS or IAS, they did so with great aspirations and a genuine desire to serve the country. Today, however, they are being used and misused like pawns in what resembles a mafia gang," he said.

Appealing to people across the country, Wangchuk said such practices must stop, asserting that India, as the world's largest democracy, must uphold constitutional values and ensure that police officers and government officials are not used for unlawful actions.

"I have appealed to President Murmu and the prime minister to put an end to this lawlessness and ensure that our officers and police personnel are allowed to discharge their duties with dignity and within the bounds of the law," he said.

Wangchuk also defended the ongoing sit-in protest, saying he had joined his colleagues at the protest site and that the demonstration, which had continued for 10 days, was peaceful and authorised.

Turning to the upcoming LAHDC elections, he renewed his appeal to the government not to hold the polls during winter, arguing that a substantial section of the population would be outside Ladakh and unable to participate.

"On the one hand, we send a message to the world that we take democracy to the last citizen, even flying helicopters to polling stations where there are just two voters. On the other hand, we are excluding 40 to 50 per cent of the population and conducting elections during winter, amid snowfall, while also subjecting government officials to immense hardship," he said.

Wangchuk maintained that people were not opposed to elections but wanted them conducted during a season conducive to public participation and the smooth deployment of officials, particularly in remote and snowbound areas.

He said the government should reconsider its approach and ensure that democratic processes in Ladakh were inclusive rather than imposed on the people.

data.title: Delhi Jal Board plans to monetise land and buildings for revenue generation
data.description:
In an attempt to generate revenue, the Delhi Jal Board plans to monetise its land and buildings to private companies, starting with 'Varunalay', its headquarters situated in Karol Bagh, officials said on Saturday.

Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has around 27 lakh water connections across the city , however the water utility has been reeling under financial losses for the past several years.

"In a recent board meeting the proposal to monetise its properties including land and buildings has been approved. We plan to hire a Department of Economic Affairs-empanelled financial advisor to carry out an assessment and submit a report," an official said.

 

To begin with, the Delhi Jal Board's land and building assets for the Jhandewalan office -- Varunalaya, Haiderpur WTP Residential housing -- Varun Niketan and Jal Vihar situated in Lajpat Nagar, will be monetised.

"Following this we plan to identify other assets that can also be commercialised," an official said.

Located in busy commercial area of Karol Bagh the 'Varunalaya' has six floors, divided into three phases, where the DJB Chief Executive Officer, other Chief Engineers and DJB board members operate. In Lajpat Nagar, the DJB mostly has residential properties for its officers and an old pump house.

Officials added that water tariffs have not been increased since 2018, which is affecting the financial health of the DJB, as loans and interest of the board have surpassed Rs 73,000 crore.

data.title: Maha FDA suspends Amazon, BigBasket Pune dark stores over safety violations
data.description:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Saturday suspended the food licences of Amazon and BigBasket dark stores located on Sinhagad Road in Pune city after finding "serious violations" of food safety and hygiene norms, officials said.

The action was taken under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, after officials found expired food products, unhygienic conditions and violations of Schedule IV provisions at both establishments during their inspections, they said.

Dark stores are retail or warehouse-like facilities designed exclusively for fulfilling online orders. They are neighbourhood micro-fulfilment centres closed to walk-in shoppers that store high-demand items to power ultra-fast online deliveries.

 

During an inspection at the Amazon dark store operated by Gajanan Inventories, officials found expired laddoos, pedhas and other food products. They also observed fungus growing on expired products, and dust in food containers. A ghee container had a broken lid and oil was leaking from the cartons, officials said.

Improper pest control measures and a lack of records related to personnel hygiene and sanitation were also found. Food and non-food items, including soap and ghee containers, were found stored together, they said.

At the BigBasket dark store operated by Innovative Retail Concept, officials found expired cakes, bread, milk rusk and chutney, and observed other food safety violations.

Food products were found lying on the floor.

The inspection also found a broken floor, an unhygienic cold room, leaking oil packets and improper pest control measures. Food and non-food items were found stored together, the officials said.

The action was carried out by Food Safety Officer Supriya Jagtap under the guidance of Assistant Commissioner (Food) Narayan Sarkate and the leadership of Joint Commissioner (Food) Shrikant Karkale.

Karkale said the FDA would take strict action against establishments found compromising consumer health and violating food safety regulations. He warned food businesses, including hotels, to strictly follow licence conditions, hygiene standards and food storage norms, failing which their licences could be suspended or cancelled.

data.title: COP31 climate talks extend into overtime amid deadlock on fossil fuels
data.description:
Work crews were boxing up the venue of this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkiye, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will result in concrete plans to drastically slash the use of fossil fuels.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, called COP31, which was supposed to end Friday, drew strong condemnation from activists and some countries for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The final document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which is contributing to devastating heat waves, floods and other disasters.

 

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In the lead up to these talks, the UN announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

"No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be," said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.

Climate talks go into overtime

Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the "pavilions," where countries showcased their climate policies and hosted panel discussions, workers were packing up electronics and other belongings Saturday morning.

The hallways, normally bustling with participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos in front of the deserted pavilions.

"COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier," said Rachel Cleetus from the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.

Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters -- including this year's heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal -- become more deadly.

Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to UN funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.

The United States, a major polluter and the world's largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks.

Next year's climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

Criticism of COP31 grows

On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan "you are killing the future" interrupted official COP proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting "You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait." The Global South is a term that isn't geographical, but a reference to developing countries in general.

"You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now," the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the room by security.

The demonstration interrupted Turkiye's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said "let's try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks.

"Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it's nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here watching the negotiations and waiting for the next iteration of the text," said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.

"We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on," he said.

data.title: Shivakumar urges ASHA workers to end protest, promises permanent solution
data.description:
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar on Saturday appealed to protesting ASHA workers to call off their agitation, assuring them that the government was considering a comprehensive and permanent solution to their demands.

In a post on X, Shivakumar said the government stood with the workers and would take appropriate steps after discussing their demands with the Cabinet.

Making an appeal on behalf of the government, he said he understood the difficulties and hardships they were facing while fighting for their demands.

"It pains me to see you fighting day and night, staying away from your families. You are not just ASHA workers to me; you are like my own sisters," he said.

 

The CM reiterated that the government was considering a comprehensive and permanent solution to their demands in the coming days.

"We stand with you and will discuss the matter with the Cabinet and take appropriate steps," he said.

"As an elder brother, I appeal to you to kindly respond to my request and call off your protest. We respect your service, hard work and sacrifices. The government is committed to addressing your demands and providing an appropriate solution," he added.

Despite repeated appeals from the government to withdraw their agitation, the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) workers have continued their protest, maintaining that they would call it off only after the government issued a specific order addressing their demands.

The workers began an indefinite day-and-night protest at Freedom Park on Tuesday, demanding that the government fix their monthly honorarium at Rs 15,000 and address their other pending demands.

They have also reportedly raised concerns over the non-payment of honoraria for work related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the educational and social survey.

data.title: Ashok Leyland to set up truck plant in Singur, work to begin soon: Minister
data.description:
Union Minister Sukanta Majumdar on Saturday said commercial vehicle manufacturer Ashok Leyland would set up a truck manufacturing plant in Singur, with work on the project expected to begin soon, reviving hopes of industrialisation at the site where the Tata Nano project was abandoned nearly two decades ago.

Speaking to reporters after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's programme at IIT Kharagpur, Majumdar said the BJP government was committed to bringing industry to Singur and that the proposed facility would manufacture heavy vehicles.

"We want to bring industry back to Singur. Our chief minister has also said so. I am reiterating today that Ashok Leyland is coming to Singur. It will set up a truck manufacturing plant, and work will begin soon," the Union minister of state for education said.

 

The announcement follows Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari's statement on November 5 that his government had held preliminary discussions with Ashok Leyland for setting up a heavy vehicle manufacturing unit in Singur.

Adhikari had then cautioned against making premature announcements, stressing that the government would prioritise projects capable of actual implementation over publicity-driven memorandums of understanding.

The latest announcement signals the BJP government's attempt to turn Singur, once synonymous with the collapse of a major industrial investment, into a showcase of its industrial revival agenda in West Bengal.

However, the project is yet to be formally detailed, with no investment outlay, employment projections or implementation timeline announced so far.

Majumdar also blamed successive state governments for Bengal missing out on major industrial opportunities, citing the semiconductor industry as an example.

"Taiwan is where it is today in the semiconductor industry, a position we could have occupied. The opportunity had come to us earlier, but the government of that time opposed computers, and consequently the semiconductor industry did not come up," he said, targeting the erstwhile Left Front government.

He also accused the Trinamool Congress government of failing to translate its industrialisation promises into concrete projects.

Singur's industrial future remains politically significant in Bengal, where the withdrawal of Tata Motors' Nano project in 2008 became a turning point in the state's politics.

The Left Front government, led by then Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee, had acquired around 997 acres for the proposed small-car factory.

A prolonged anti land acquisition agitation led by Mamata Banerjee, then the opposition leader, against the acquisition of farmland forced Tata Motors to abandon the project and shift it to Sanand in Gujarat.

The agitation helped propel Banerjee's Trinamool Congress to power in 2011, ending the Left Front's 34-year rule.

Her government subsequently returned the acquired land to unwilling farmers following a Supreme Court verdict, while the abandoned factory infrastructure was dismantled.

Nearly 18 years after the Nano project's exit, the proposed Ashok Leyland facility offers the BJP an opportunity to politically recast Singur as a symbol of industrial revival.

The project's credibility, however, will ultimately depend on translating the announcement into a concrete investment and a functioning manufacturing unit.
